value.region_notes_beginner: In the Las Vegas Valley you grow habanero as a single spring crop, and it is the tightest fit of the Nevada pepper group. Start seed indoors in early February and set transplants out in mid-March once frost is past, same as the other peppers, but because habanero needs about 95 days to first color, harvest does not begin until mid-June, close to the summer heat wall. The Las Vegas Valley (zone 9) gets about two and a half weeks of picking before the heat locks in at the start of July; the cooler zone 8 edge, which transplants later, gets barely two weeks, with the last of it ripening as the heat_pause begins. There is no fall replanting here, so choose a quicker pepper if you want a longer harvest, or plant habanero at the earliest safe date to get the most out of the window.
value.region_notes_seasoned: The Las Vegas Valley (Mojave high desert) runs habanero on one spring cycle, per University of Nevada, Reno Extension, and it is the most marginal fit of the region's Shape A peppers. This crop's own heat_threshold_f (about 95°F) is the highest of the group, but Southern Nevada's dry summer heat still exceeds it from June into September. At a 95-day days_to_maturity_mid anchored to the front of the transplant window, first color lands in mid-June in zone 9 and late June in the later-transplanted zone 8; both zones get a genuinely short harvest, with fruit already set continuing to ripen a few days into the July heat_pause before the plant stops producing. Zone 10 (Laughlin) fares no better despite its earlier frost-free start: its own June heat_pause onset caps the window to about ten days in late May. Judgment call: harvest_start is anchored to the earliest edge of the plant_out window rather than its midpoint (unlike the other five Shape A crops here), specifically so habanero keeps a real, if short, harvest month before the heat_pause claims the rest; no fall replant per SP-99-11/FS-02-61, so gardeners wanting a longer habanero harvest should budget for a notably shorter Nevada season than habanero gives in a milder climate.

value.region_notes_beginner: In the Las Vegas Valley okra is a true summer crop. Direct-sow seed anytime from early March through May, once the soil has warmed, and the plants keep making pods right through the hottest part of the year. Pick every day or two once they start (pods go from tender to woody fast), and expect the harvest to run from early May clear into November, only stopping when frost finally arrives. Nothing else in the desert garden shrugs off 100°F days like okra does.
value.region_notes_seasoned: Southern Nevada's summer heat is exactly what okra wants, so the UNLV/UNR Cooperative Extension Master Gardener planting chart gives it one of the valley's widest warm-season windows, direct-sown March through May with no indoor start needed. Unlike the desert's fruiting nightshades, okra keeps setting pods straight through the June to September heat wall with no pause, so harvest runs continuously from about eight to nine weeks after the earliest sowing until frost shuts it down (late November in the valley, a couple weeks earlier at the cooler zone 8 fringe, early December at Laughlin in zone 10). Succession-sow through May to keep pods coming without a gap.

8.day_length_note_seasoned: At the Las Vegas Valley's latitude, about 36 degrees N, grow intermediate-day onions such as Candy or Super Star, which bulb at around 12 to 14 hours of daylight. They are set out in fall or late winter and bulb as days lengthen through spring. A long-day (northern) variety here rarely reaches its longer daylength trigger and bulbs poorly, while a short-day variety may bulb too early and small.
8.day_length_note_beginner: Where you live, plant intermediate-day onions like Candy or Super Star. A northern long-day onion planted here would struggle to bulb, and a far-southern short-day one bulbs too early.

8.day_length_note_seasoned: At the Las Vegas Valley's latitude, about 36 degrees N, grow intermediate-day onions such as Candy or Super Star, which bulb at around 12 to 14 hours of daylight. A long-day (northern) variety here rarely reaches its longer daylength trigger and bulbs poorly, while a short-day variety may bulb too early and small.
8.day_length_note_beginner: Where you live, plant intermediate-day onions like Candy or Super Star. 8.notes: Plant one clump inside a pot or a buried, bottomless barrier so mint's spreading roots stay contained. In the Las Vegas Valley's dry heat, mint runs as a cool-season crop: establish a division or cutting in early fall, harvest fall through spring, and pause through the extreme summer, when even heavy shade and constant water struggle to keep it going. Keep the soil evenly moist and pinch flower buds to keep leaves tender.

Unlike bee balm and mint, echinacea is drought-tolerant and thrives through the Mojave summer once established, so no heat_pause is carried (a deliberate divergence from the low_desert_az cell, which hedges it as marginal; the desert's dryness, not its heat, was that cell's real caveat, and appropriate siting and deep infrequent watering answer it).

8.notes: Echinacea is drought-tolerant and does well in the Las Vegas Valley once established: set out a division, transplant, or stratified seedling in spring in full sun and sharp drainage, water deeply but infrequently, and it blooms from early summer into fall without the heat exclusion moisture-hungry perennials need here. Leave cones standing into winter for the birds, then cut back in late winter; divide an established clump every 3 to 4 years.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Las Vegas Valley winters bank enough chill for low and moderate chill apples; the University of Nevada, Reno field trial confirms the crop fruits dependably here when the variety is matched to the chill (see the variety guidance). Summer heat and sunburn on young bark, not frost, are the practical hazards; early bloom in March clears the late-February last frost in most years.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Apples fruit reliably in Las Vegas if you pick a low or moderate chill variety the local trial confirmed. Heat, not cold, is the thing to manage; shade young trunks their first summers.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Bloom in early March usually clears the late-February last frost; an unusually late cold snap during bloom is an occasional, not typical, risk. Heat and sunburn are the larger hazards here.

8.suitability_note_seasoned: The cooler, higher zone 8 pockets bank more chill (roughly 500 to 900 hours), clearing the moderate chill varieties comfortably and edging toward the lower end of the high-chill group; bloom runs a couple of weeks later than the valley floor, after the mid-March last frost.
8.suitability_note_beginner: The higher, cooler parts of the region get more winter chill, so a wider range of apples fruits well. Bloom comes a little later here, after the March frost.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Bloom in April clears the mid-March last frost in most years; a late frost at the higher elevations during bloom is the occasional risk to watch.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: Laughlin and the warm Colorado River corner (zone 10) bank the least chill, roughly 150 to 450 hours, so only the lowest-chill varieties (Anna, Dorsett Golden, Ein Shemer) fruit dependably; the moderate and high-chill sorts are unreliable this warm. Heat and sunburn are the dominant hazards.
10.suitability_note_beginner: It is warmest at Laughlin, with the least winter chill, so stick to the lowest-chill apples like Anna and Dorsett Golden. Heat is the main challenge.
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is rarely the problem at Laughlin; intense summer heat and sunburn on young bark are the real hazards, and low winter chill limits the variety list.

value.region_notes_beginner: Apples grow well in the Las Vegas Valley if you choose the right variety. A University of Nevada field trial confirmed dependable performers like Dorsett Golden, Anna, Pink Lady, Fuji, Mutsu, and Granny Smith; the highest-chill types like Honeycrisp and McIntosh need more winter cold than the desert reliably gives. Plant a bare-root or container tree while it is dormant, from late fall through winter, and shade young trunks against the summer sun.
value.region_notes_seasoned: The Las Vegas Valley (Mojave high desert) fruits apple dependably when the variety is matched to the region's chill, per a University of Nevada, Reno Extension field trial at the North Las Vegas Research Orchard. Zone 9 banks roughly 300 to 700 chill hours; the trial's confirmed performers (Dorsett Golden, Pink Lady, and Mutsu as top choices, plus Anna, Fuji, and Granny Smith) span the low to moderate chill range, while the high-chill quarter of the standard variety list is unproven here. Bloom runs early, from late February at Laughlin through April in the cooler zone 8 pockets, and fruit ripens across summer. Heat and sunburn on young bark, not frost, are the main constraints. Plant bare-root or container trees during the dormant season.
value.chill_basis_seasoned: The Las Vegas Valley banks roughly 300 to 700 chill hours in zone 9, more in the cooler, higher zone 8 pockets and less at Laughlin in zone 10, enough to fruit a real range of low and moderate chill apples but not the highest-chill sorts. A University of Nevada, Reno Extension field trial at the North Las Vegas Research Orchard (2005 to 2018) confirms the dependable performers here: Dorsett Golden, Anna, Pink Lady, Mutsu, Fuji, and Granny Smith all fruit, with Dorsett Golden, Pink Lady, and Mutsu rated top choices, and the low-chill Ein Shemer, Dolgo, and Gala sit comfortably under the confirmed range. The high-chill varieties, McIntosh, Honeycrisp, Zestar!, Empire, Golden Delicious, Jonagold, and Liberty, all need about 700 hours or more and are unproven for the Las Vegas Valley; the trial did not confirm them, so treat them as a gamble here rather than a recommendation.
value.chill_basis_beginner: The desert here gives a few hundred chill hours, enough for low and moderate chill apples. Choose the varieties a University of Nevada field trial confirmed for Las Vegas, such as Dorsett Golden, Anna, Pink Lady, Fuji, Mutsu, and Granny Smith. The highest-chill types like Honeycrisp, McIntosh, and Golden Delicious need more winter cold than the valley reliably gives, so they are not a safe bet here.

8.suitability_note_seasoned: The cooler, higher zone 8 pockets bank roughly 500 to 900 chill hours, clearing the entire recommended list here, including the higher chill Chinese (Mormon) and Goldrich. Bloom runs into March and April, later than the valley floor, which trims the late frost risk somewhat even though the growing season starts later.
8.suitability_note_beginner: The higher, cooler parts of the region get more winter chill, so every apricot variety here has a good chance, even higher chill kinds like Moorpark and Chinese (Mormon). Bloom comes a little later, which helps dodge frost.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Bloom in March and April usually clears the mid March last frost; an unusually late cold snap during bloom is the occasional risk to watch, more so at the higher elevations.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 (the Las Vegas Valley floor) banks roughly 300 to 700 chill hours, enough to fruit apricot dependably with the right variety: Katy, Blenheim, Tilton, Moorpark, and Harglow all clear the band, while the 700 hour Chinese (Mormon) and Goldrich sit at the ceiling and are the first to disappoint in a mild winter. Bloom in late February to March is early enough that a late cold snap is an occasional risk; the dry air otherwise keeps disease low.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Apricots fruit reliably in the Las Vegas Valley if you choose a low or moderate chill variety like Katy, Blenheim, Tilton, Moorpark, or Harglow. Bloom comes early, so watch for a late frost, but the dry air means disease is rarely the problem.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Bloom in late February to March occasionally meets a late valley frost; more years than not it clears, and the dry air otherwise keeps disease pressure low.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: Laughlin and the Colorado River corner (zone 10) bank the least chill, roughly 150 to 450 hours, so only the lowest chill varieties, Katy and Blenheim, fruit dependably; Tilton, Moorpark, Harglow, and the 700 hour Chinese (Mormon) and Goldrich need more cold than this warm corner reliably banks. Bloom is very early here, mid February into March; summer heat and sunburn on young bark are the bigger concern than frost.
10.suitability_note_beginner: It is warmest at Laughlin, with the least winter chill, so stick to Katy or Blenheim. Heat and sun, not frost, are the main challenge here.
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is rarely the limit at Laughlin; low winter chill for the higher chill varieties, and intense summer heat, are the real constraints.

value.region_notes_beginner: Apricots do well across the Las Vegas Valley region if you match the variety to your zone. Katy and Blenheim are the safest, lowest chill picks and will fruit everywhere in the region, including the warm Laughlin corner. Moorpark, Tilton, and Harglow need more winter cold and are better suited to the valley floor and the cooler zone 8 pockets. Plant a bare root or container tree while it is dormant, from December through February, and watch for a late frost on the early bloom.
value.region_notes_seasoned: Apricot fruits reliably across the Las Vegas Valley region when the variety is matched to the zone's chill. Zone 9 banks roughly 300 to 700 chill hours, enough for Katy, Blenheim, Tilton, Moorpark, and Harglow, with the 700 hour Chinese (Mormon) and Goldrich right at the edge. The cooler zone 8 pockets clear the whole list with margin, while the warm Laughlin corner (zone 10) reliably suits only the lowest chill picks, Katy and Blenheim. Bloom comes very early (mid February through March depending on zone), which puts the crop at some risk from a late frost; the dry desert air otherwise keeps disease pressure low, so heat and sunburn on young bark, not brown rot, are the summer concern. Plant bare root or container trees during the dormant season.
value.chill_basis_seasoned: The Las Vegas Valley banks roughly 300 to 700 chill hours in zone 9, more in the cooler zone 8 pockets and less at Laughlin in zone 10. That covers a genuine spread of apricot chill needs: Katy (about 350 hours), Blenheim (450), Tilton and Harglow (600 to 650), and Moorpark (650) all fit zone 9 with room to spare, while Chinese (Mormon) and Goldrich sit right at the 700 hour ceiling, workable most years but the first to miss in a warm winter. Zone 8's wider band clears the whole list comfortably. 9.type_note_seasoned: Blackberry is marginal in the Mojave: summer highs routinely top 100°F from June into September (UNR Cooperative Extension FS-02-61), stressing canes and scorching ripening fruit. No Nevada-specific cultivar trial covers blackberry, so this guide steers toward heat-tolerant, low-chill, primocane (fall-bearing) types over standard floricane cultivars; give the planting afternoon shade and steady, generous water, and expect a smaller, harder-won crop than in a milder climate.
9.type_note_beginner: Blackberry is a stretch in the Mojave's desert heat, which regularly tops 100°F for months at a time. Choose a heat-tolerant, low-chill, fall-bearing type, plant it where it gets afternoon shade, and water it generously. Do not expect a bumper crop here.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is rarely the limiting factor for blackberry in the Mojave; the intense, months-long summer heat is what threatens the planting, so siting for afternoon shade matters more than frost protection.
9.grown_as_note_seasoned: Here a blackberry is grown as a deciduous cane fruit: the canes drop their leaves through the mild Mojave winter while the perennial crown lives for 15 to 20 years, and each cane lives only two, growing one year and fruiting the next before dying. Prune in the dormant season, matching the cut to the cultivar's habit. Planted once, a patch can fruit for two decades if it is sited to survive the desert summers.
9.grown_as_note_beginner: Your blackberry loses its leaves and rests through the mild desert winter (this rest is called dormancy). The roots live for years, but each cane lives only two: it grows one year, then fruits and dies. Prune it in winter, and plant once for a patch that can keep producing for many years if you manage the summer heat.

9.type_note_seasoned: Raspberry is marginal in the Mojave: the Las Vegas Valley's intense, months-long summer heat, routinely above 100°F June through September (UNR Cooperative Extension FS-02-61), and the desert's dry air both work against it. No Nevada-specific cultivar trial exists, but the heat-tolerant, low-chill, fall-bearing (primocane) types recommended across the hot desert Southwest are the best bet here; plant where it gets afternoon shade, mulch heavily, and water steadily. Expect a smaller, shorter-lived planting than in a cooler climate.
9.type_note_beginner: Raspberry is a tough crop for the Las Vegas Valley's desert heat. Choose a heat-tolerant, low-chill, fall-bearing type, give it afternoon shade and deep mulch, and water it steadily. It will not be an easy or long-lived planting here.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is rarely the issue for raspberry in the Mojave; relentless heat, intense sun, and dry air are what stress the canes, so shade and water matter far more than frost protection.
9.grown_as_note_seasoned: In the Mojave a raspberry is grown as a deciduous, heat-tolerant cane fruit, planted while dormant in winter; it blooms in late winter to early spring and ripens before the worst heat arrives, then is pruned and retrained in the dormant season. Only low-chill, heat-tolerant types persist here, and even those are best treated as a short-lived planting rather than a dependable one.
9.grown_as_note_beginner: In the Mojave, raspberries are grown as a heat-tolerant type, planted in winter while dormant. They flower in late winter to early spring and ripen before the worst heat. Only special low-chill types will keep going here, and even those may not last many years.

9.type_note_seasoned: American elderberry is the type to grow; there is no separate low-chill or desert-adapted type. It can grow and fruit in the Las Vegas Valley with irrigation, but it is a moisture-loving shrub native to far wetter ground than the desert offers on its own, so it depends entirely on steady, generous watering and benefits from afternoon shade through the worst of the summer heat, which routinely tops 100°F June through September (UNR Cooperative Extension FS-02-61). Plant two different cultivars for cross-pollination.
9.type_note_beginner: American elderberry is the one type to grow here. It can produce in the Las Vegas Valley, but only with consistent watering, since it naturally grows in much wetter places than the desert. Give it afternoon shade in summer and plant two different varieties.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is rarely the limiting factor for elderberry in the Mojave; keeping the plant watered through the long, intense summer heat is the real management task.
9.grown_as_note_seasoned: Elderberry is a permanent deciduous shrub here too, planted once and kept for years, though in the mild Mojave winters it rests only briefly. It blooms in spring and ripens earlier than in a cooler climate; keep it well watered through the heat, renew old canes in late winter, and plant two different cultivars for good fruit set.
9.grown_as_note_beginner: Your elderberry is a long-lived bush you plant once and keep for years. Keep it well watered in the heat, prune old stems in late winter, and plant two different varieties.

value.region_notes_seasoned: Elderberry is marginal across the Nevada high desert: American elderberry, the only type grown here, is a moisture-loving shrub native to far wetter ground than the Mojave offers on its own, so it depends entirely on steady, generous irrigation rather than on any particular chill or type choice. 9.type_note_seasoned: Blueberry is very marginal in the Las Vegas Valley low desert, and the limiting factor is not chill but soil: blueberries need acidic soil around pH 4.5 to 5.5, and the Mojave's native soil is strongly alkaline, hostile ground for this plant. Grow only the lowest-chill southern highbush selections, only in large containers filled with an amended acidic mix (peat or pine bark), acidify the irrigation water, and give afternoon shade through the summer heat. Even then, treat any harvest as a bonus, not a dependable crop.
9.type_note_beginner: Blueberry is a very hard sell in the Las Vegas Valley. The real problem is the soil: it is too alkaline (not acidic enough) for blueberries, which need acidic soil to thrive. Grow a low-chill variety in a large container filled with a special acidic potting mix, never in the ground, water it with acidified water, and give it shade in summer. Expect this to be a fussy experiment, not a sure harvest.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is rarely the limiting factor for blueberry in the low desert; alkaline soil, extreme summer heat, and marginal winter chill are the binding constraints, so an early harvest before the worst heat matters more than frost protection.
9.grown_as_note_seasoned: In the Las Vegas Valley low desert, blueberry is a container-only crop, since the native soil is too alkaline for in-ground planting; grown in pots, it stays mild enough through the winter that this guide treats it as evergreen here, keeping its leaves year round. The year runs from a winter bloom to an early harvest, April into May, then a care period of light shaping, feeding, and acidified watering. Shield it from extreme heat.
9.grown_as_note_beginner: In the Las Vegas Valley, blueberries have to be grown in large containers because the ground soil is too alkaline. Grown that way, it is a long-lived bush that stays green year round in this mild-winter zone. It flowers in winter and ripens berries in spring, around April to May, then settles into a calmer stretch of light care and careful watering. Protect it from the harshest heat.

8.type_note_seasoned: Blueberry is still very marginal in the cooler zone 8 pockets: the alkaline Mojave soil is just as hostile here as on the valley floor, so blueberry still needs a large container filled with an amended acidic mix and acidified irrigation water regardless of elevation. The extra winter chill at this elevation lets the plant go properly dormant and supports a wider range of southern highbush selections, but soil, not cold, remains the binding constraint. Expect a genuine experiment, not a dependable harvest.

8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: A late-winter freeze can still occur into March at this elevation, so the early bloom of low-chill cultivars carries some risk; favor later-blooming selections and cover containers during a hard cold snap.

It breaks bud and blooms in spring, when an open flower can be caught by a late freeze, then ripens fruit May into June. Prune late in dormancy, just before bud break.

plant_out.label: establishment
plant_out.synthesis_note: Set dormant or young strawberry plants in fall, the Southern Nevada window on the UNLV/UNR Cooperative Extension Master Gardener planting chart for the Las Vegas Valley (unlv_mg_svn). Strawberries are grown here as a cool-season annual, not a perennial bed: plants set in fall fruit the following winter and spring, then are pulled before the summer heat, which is too intense to carry a planting.

bloom.label: establishment
bloom.synthesis_note: Flowering builds through the cool winter and into early spring on the fall-set planting, once short autumn day lengths have triggered flower-bud formation.

harvest_start.label: establishment
harvest_start.synthesis_note: Harvest begins as the plants finish flowering and the weather warms toward the ideal fruiting range, well before the desert heat sets in.

harvest_end.label: establishment
harvest_end.synthesis_note: Fruiting finishes before temperatures climb past the roughly 90°F ceiling above which plants stop growing well (UNR Extension FS-02-61); the planting is then pulled and discarded, and fresh plants are set the following fall.

9.grown_as_note_seasoned: The Las Vegas Valley grows strawberries as a cool-season annual, not a perennial bed: plants do not grow well above about 90°F (UNR Cooperative Extension FS-02-61), so a planting set in fall fruits through the mild winter and into spring, then is pulled before the desert's summer heat arrives, with fresh plants set again the next fall. Set dormant or young plants from September into November, the Southern Nevada window on the UNLV/UNR Cooperative Extension Master Gardener planting chart, and choose a site with morning sun but afternoon shade to ease heat and water stress. Grow on well-drained beds, since strawberries are sensitive to salty soil and irrigation water.
9.grown_as_note_beginner: In the Las Vegas Valley, strawberries are a winter crop you grow and then replace, not a bed that lives for years. Plant in fall, from around September into November, pick berries from late winter into spring, then pull the plants before the hot summer and start fresh again the next fall. Give them morning sun with afternoon shade, and plant them where water drains away well.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: A handful of freezing nights occur in December and January (NWS Las Vegas frost normals). Open blossoms and ripening fruit are damaged below 32°F, so on a night a hard freeze is forecast during bloom, cover the bed with frost cloth beforehand and anchor the edges.

8.grown_as_note_seasoned: The cooler zone 8 pockets grow strawberries the same cool-season annual way, just on a slightly later, longer clock: plants do not grow well above about 90°F (UNR Cooperative Extension FS-02-61), so a planting set in early fall, ahead of this zone's earlier first frost, fruits through winter into a spring that runs a little later than the valley floor before being pulled and replanted the next fall. Choose a site with morning sun but afternoon shade, and grow on well-drained beds.
8.grown_as_note_beginner: In the cooler zone 8 pockets, strawberries are grown the same winter-crop way as the rest of the region, just started a little earlier in fall and harvested a little later in spring. Plant in September to October, pick berries into early summer, then pull the plants and start fresh the next fall. Give them morning sun with afternoon shade.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: The cooler zone 8 pockets see more freezing nights, and the last frost runs into mid-March, later into the bloom window than on the valley floor. Open blossoms and ripening fruit are damaged below 32°F, so keep frost cloth on hand through the whole bloom period, not just the earliest weeks.

value.region_notes_beginner: In the Las Vegas Valley region, strawberries are a winter crop you grow and then replace, not a bed that lives for years. Plant transplants in fall, roughly September into November (a little earlier, September into October, in the cooler zone 8 pockets), on beds where water drains away well. Pick berries from late winter into spring, then pull the plants out when the hot summer arrives and plant fresh ones the next fall, because young plants make the best fruit. value.region_notes_seasoned: The Nevada high desert grows strawberries as a cool-season annual, not a perennial bed, the same desert pattern this crop follows in the Arizona low desert. Plants do not grow well above about 90°F (UNR Cooperative Extension FS-02-61), so set transplants in fall, September into November on the Las Vegas Valley floor and the Laughlin corner (a little earlier, September into October, in the cooler zone 8 pockets), per the UNLV/UNR Cooperative Extension Master Gardener Southern Nevada planting chart. Fruit the planting through the mild winter and into spring, then pull and discard it before summer heat arrives and replant fresh the following fall, since the best fruit comes from young plants. Choose a site with morning sun but afternoon shade, grow on well-drained beds, and keep frost cloth on hand for freezing nights during bloom, since open blossoms are damaged below 32°F.

patches.from: T1-SOURCED (Phase A chill-sourcing, 2026-06-24). Model: Utah / modified-Weinberger chill hours, accumulated hours with temperature between 32 and 45 degrees F over the winter dormant season (the model the cited extensions use and the definition carried in this dataset's chill prose). One crop-invariant winter-chill-DELIVERED band per region+zone, reconciled to published T1 extension chill-accumulation data, NEVER derived from the USDA winter-low zone. Sources by region: northern_tier / ca_interior reconciled to UC Davis Fruit & Nut Research & Information Center chill-accumulation data (ucd_fruitnut); ca_north_coast / ca_south_coast / ca_desert to UC ANR and UC Statewide IPM California chill data (ucanr_ext, uc_ipm); se_gulf to University of Georgia Cooperative Extension chill-hour station data (uga_ext); warm_arid to Texas A&M AgriLife Extension Texas chill-hour maps and University of Arizona Cooperative Extension elevation chill bands (tamu_agrilife, uarizona_ext); low_desert_az to University of Arizona Cooperative Extension low-desert chill data (uarizona_ext); fl_peninsula / hawaii_tropical to UF/IFAS Extension low-chill and near-zero-chill data (uf_ifas_hs1153). rgv (2026-07-13, RGV / subtropical-South-Texas region arc, zones 9-10) reconciled to Texas A&M AgriLife Extension South Texas / Lower Rio Grande Valley chill-hour guidance (tamu_agrilife): AgriLife Extension horticulturist Larry Stein places Rio Grande Valley orchard chill requirements at roughly 200 to 300 chill hours, and the Valley's subtropical, near-frost-free winters (about 340 frost-free days) bank essentially no chill in warm winters, so the delivered band is [0, 300] for both zone 9 and zone 10, corroborated by LSU AgCenter's 200 to 300 chill-hour figure for the comparably subtropical coastal-south-Louisiana Gulf climate (lsu_agcenter); RGV sits just above the deep-tropical fl_peninsula z11 / hawaii_tropical [0, 150] floor and below the se_gulf band, and the 0 low edge (warm winters bank near-zero chill) is what drives the A3 no-fruit split for temperate stone and pome fruit. Bands are the climate's typical winter delivery envelope, widened across zones where station data and crop-author estimates differ; per-variety chill-REQUIRED (chill_hours_required / chill_hours_range) is the separate axis and is unchanged. pnw (2026-07-14, maritime Pacific Northwest region arc, Task 3, zones 8-9) reconciled to WSU Skagit County Extension / WSU Mount Vernon NWREC: Skagit Valley AWN (Agricultural Weather Network) station data, 2007-2015, banks 968 to 1950 chill hours annually (average ~1468) -- Hunter, 'The Importance of Chilling,' WSU Skagit County Extension, 2016. Model: Utah / modified-Weinberger chill hours, accumulated hours with temperature between 32 and 45 degrees F over the winter dormant season (the model already carried in this table's definition); note the WSU Skagit source itself flags that its own station figure uses a simpler 'hour below 45 degF' proxy rather than the strict 32-45 degF window, a close but not identical match in a maritime winter that rarely sustains long stretches below 32 degF. pnw z8 (Puget Sound / Willamette Valley lowlands, e.g. Skagit Valley / Mount Vernon WA, the WSU NWREC station site) is the direct station-sourced band: [968, 1950]. pnw z9 (milder coastal / protected pockets, e.g. immediate WA/OR coast) has no distinct T1 station chill figure located in this pass; [700, 1500] is a reasoned, deliberately conservative-lower-bounded estimate from the same 32-45 degF model and the same general maritime winter regime -- milder coastal minimum temperatures (per the zone's own extreme-minimum-temperature definition) do not necessarily mean less time spent in the 32-45 degF chill window, since maritime marine-layer winters characteristically linger in that cool damp band rather than swinging to hard freeze or above-45 degF warmth. This z9 band is an ESTIMATE, not a station-sourced figure, and should be tightened with a direct coastal-station chill record (e.g. an OSU Aurora/Willamette Valley or immediate-coast Oregon/Washington station) before it backs a z9-specific per-variety chill-required certification claim. Both bands clear the ~600-1000 hour fruiting threshold comfortably and sit far above rgv's near-frost-free [0,300] floor, consistent with the maritime PNW's well-documented reputation among temperate tree-fruit and small-fruit growers for reliable, ample winter chill (unlike se_gulf [650,1000] or ca_interior [500,1100] at the same zone-8 label -- the maritime PNW's long, mild, damp winters bank more chill than either despite sharing a zone number, because continental/subtropical climates swing through the 32-45 degF band quickly rather than lingering in it). z8's low bound (968) exceeds z9's low bound (700), matching the convention used elsewhere in this table that the colder-lowland-winter zone carries the higher chill floor. Per-variety chill-REQUIRED (chill_hours_required / chill_hours_range) is the separate axis and is unchanged by this addition. Chilling hours (hours near 35 to 45 degrees F during winter dormancy) are abundant across the Mid-Atlantic and do not limit tree fruit here. The warmer Coastal Plain and Tidewater (zone 8) banks in excess of 1,000 hours; the cooler Piedmont, Maryland, New Jersey, and Pennsylvania (zone 7) banks more, on the order of 1,400 hours by the end of March. Every zone clears the chilling requirement of the standard 750 to 1,000 hour tree-fruit varieties. Sources: NC State Extension Gardener Handbook ch. 15 (>1,000 hours annually statewide); Penn State, Make Like a Tree and Chill (over 1,400 chill hours by the end of March); Virginia Cooperative Extension 422-025 (Virginia apples require about 1,000 hours, met comfortably); University of Maryland Extension (chill deficit is not a regional concern). Verified 2026-07-20. Chilling hours (hours near 35 to 45 degrees F during winter dormancy, Utah model) are banked across the whole Mid-South belt, but with a real intra-state gradient rather than a single flat figure. The University of Arkansas reports average accumulated chilling hours by March 1 at four stations: the northern Ozark upland (Fayetteville, zone 7) 1,024, the western station (Clarksville) 1,081, the northeastern Delta (Wynne) 1,069, and the southwestern warm edge (Hope, zone 8) 901. The cooler upland north and the delta bank on the order of 1,000 to 1,300 hours (zone 7); the warmer lowland south runs from Hope's roughly 900 hours up to about 1,100 (zone 8). Every zone clears the chilling requirement of the standard tree-fruit variety set (the highest canonical apple variety, McIntosh, needs about 900), though the southwestern warm edge clears it by the slimmest margin, so growers there should favor lower-chill varieties. Chill is a non-factor for blackberry (the belt's signature crop), which fruits many times over its requirement everywhere. Source: University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension, Chilling Hour Reports (Utah model, 1990 to 2000 baseline). Verified 2026-07-20.

value.name: UNR Extension SP-20-07, Research Orchard Fruit Evaluations & Recommendations for Southern Nevada (2020)
value.citable_for: UNR Extension specific publication SP-20-07 (M.L. Robinson, A. O'Callaghan, L. Ruskamp; peer-reviewed). Direct multi-year (2005-2018) apple variety field trial at the North Las Vegas Research Orchard (4600 Horse Drive, inside the zone 9 belt), with per-variety performance ratings and chill-hour figures. Backs the nevada apple suitability (fruits_reliably) and the reliable-vs-unproven variety steering (confirmed performers Dorsett Golden / Pink Lady / Mutsu / Anna / Fuji / Granny Smith; confirmed ceiling ~700 hr at Granny Smith). Sub-ID under unr_ext (the parent portal).

value.name: UNR/UNCE Fact Sheet FS-02-61, Home Vegetable Production in Southern Nevada
value.publisher: University of Nevada, Reno Cooperative Extension
value.citable_for: UNR Cooperative Extension Fact Sheet FS-02-61 (A.M. O'Callaghan). The Southern Nevada warm-vs-cool season planting framework: warm-season vegetables planted March through May; cool-season mid-February through April and from mid-August until the end of October; plants do not grow well above 90 degF. Backs the nevada annual season windows and the summer heat_pause. Sub-ID under unr_ext.

Verbatim extract confirmed via pypdf/fitz in the build controller env 2026-07-21: 'mid February through April and from mid August until the end of October', 'March until May', 'grow well at temperatures above 90 F'.

value.name: UNR Extension SP-99-11, Growing Tomatoes in Southern Nevada
value.citable_for: UNR Extension specific publication SP-99-11 (A. Roberts). Southern Nevada's practical last-frost date (March 15); the >90 degF-day / <55 degF-night tomato fruit-set cutoff; and the recommendation AGAINST a fall or second tomato planting for Southern Nevada (spread the single spring window by mixing early 50-60 day and main-season 80+ day varieties). Backs the nevada warm-fruiting-crop single-spring shape (no fall replant) and the heat_pause. Sub-ID under unr_ext.

value.name: Vegetable Planting Guide for Southern Nevada (Clarita Huffman, Master Gardener)
value.publisher: University of Nevada Cooperative Extension Master Gardener Program (Clark County), hosted by UNLV
value.citable_for: UNR Cooperative Extension Master Gardener (Clark County) per-crop planting chart for Southern Nevada. Cool-season crops carry a spring window (Feb-Apr) and a fall window (mid-Aug through Oct/Nov); warm-season crops a spring window (Mar-May), with quick crops (bush beans, sweet corn, cucumber, summer squash) also a late-summer (Jul-Aug) window; garlic Sept through mid-Oct; dry onions Feb plus Sept-Oct. Backs the nevada per-crop annual windows. A Master Gardener product of a T1 university extension (mirrors nmsu_donaana_mg's admission).
